Main.sentence: Delaware ( /ˈdɛləwɛər/ ⓘ ___E:DEL-ə-wair U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key)___ )  is a ___E:state U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state)___ in the ___E:Mid-Atlantic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_(United_States))___ and ___E:South Atlantic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Atlantic_states)___  regions of the United States.

It borders ___E:Maryland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland)___ to its south and west, ___E:Pennsylvania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania)___ to its north, ___E:New Jersey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey)___ to its northeast, and the ___E:Atlantic Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean)___ to its east. The state's name derives from the adjacent ___E:Delaware Bay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_Bay)___ , which in turn was named after ___E:Thomas West, 3rd Baron De La Warr U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_West,_3rd_Baron_De_La_Warr)___ , an English nobleman and the ___E:Colony of Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Virginia)___ 's first colonial-era governor.

Delaware occupies the northeastern portion of the ___E:Delmarva Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmarva_Peninsula)___ , and some islands and territory within the ___E:Delaware River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River)___ .

It is the ___E:second-smallest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_area)___ and ___E:sixth-least populous U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population)___ state, but also the ___E:sixth-most densely populated U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population_density)___ .

Delaware's most populous city is ___E:Wilmington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington,_Delaware)___ , and the state's ___E:capital U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States)___ is ___E:Dover U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover,_Delaware)___ , the second-most populous city in Delaware.

The state is divided into three counties, the fewest number of counties of any of the 50 U.S. states; from north to south, the three counties are: ___E:New Castle County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Castle_County,_Delaware)___ , ___E:Kent County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Delaware)___ , and ___E:Sussex County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex_County,_Delaware)___ .
The southern two counties, Kent and Sussex, have historically been predominantly agrarian economies.

New Castle is more ___E:urbanized U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanized_area)___ and is considered part of the ___E:Philadelphia metropolitan area U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_metropolitan_area)___ .

Delaware is considered part of the ___E:Southern United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States)___ by the ___E:U.S. Census Bureau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau)___ ,  but the state's geography, culture, and history are a hybrid of the Mid-Atlantic, ___E:Northeastern U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_United_States)___ , and Southern regions of the country.

Before the Delaware coastline was explored and developed by ___E:Europeans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_groups_in_Europe)___ in the 17th century, the state was inhabited by several ___E:Native American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States)___ tribes, including the ___E:Lenape U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape)___ in the north and ___E:Nanticoke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanticoke_people)___ in the south.

The state was first colonized by ___E:Dutch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people)___ traders at ___E:Zwaanendael U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zwaanendael_Colony)___ , near present-day ___E:Lewes, Delaware U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewes,_Delaware)___ , in 1631. Delaware was one of the ___E:Thirteen Colonies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies)___ that participated in the ___E:American Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution)___ against ___E:Great Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army_during_the_American_Revolutionary_War)___ , which established the United States as an independent nation.

On December 7, 1787, Delaware was the first state to ratify the ___E:Constitution of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States)___ , earning it the nickname "The First State".

Since the turn of the 20th century, Delaware has become an onshore ___E:corporate haven U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_haven)___ whose ___E:corporate laws U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_General_Corporation_Law)___ are deemed appealing to corporations; over half of all ___E:New York Stock Exchange U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Stock_Exchange)___ -listed corporations and over three-fifths of the ___E:Fortune 500 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_500)___ are legally incorporated in Delaware.
Over 90% of all U.S. based companies that went ___E:public U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)___ in 2021 incorporated themselves in Delaware.

Delaware was named after its location on the Delaware Bay, which in turn derived its name from ___E:Thomas West, 3rd Baron De La Warr U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_West,_3rd_Baron_De_La_Warr)___ (1577–1618), the first governor of the ___E:Colony of Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Virginia)___ .
The Delaware people, a name used by Europeans for ___E:Lenape U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape)___ people Indigenous to the Delaware Valley, also derive their name from the same source.
The name de La Warr was derived from ___E:Sussex U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex)___ and is of ___E:Anglo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England)___ -French origin.
It came probably from a ___E:Norman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_language)___ ___E:lieu-dit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieu-dit)___ La Guerre .

This ___E:toponymic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toponymic)___ likely derived from ___E:Latin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language)___ ager , the ___E:Breton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_language)___ gwern or from the ___E:Late Latin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Latin)___ varectum ( ___E:fallow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallow)___ ).

The toponyms Gara, Gare, Gaire, (the sound ___E:[ä] U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_central_unrounded_vowel)___ often mutated in ___E:[æ] U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-open_front_unrounded_vowel)___ ) also appear in historical texts cited by ___E:Lucien Musset U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien_Musset)___ , where the word ga(i)ra means ___E:gore U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gore_(road))___ .
It could also be linked with a ___E:patronymic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronymic)___ from the ___E:Old Norse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Norse)___ verr .

Before Delaware was settled by European colonists, the present-day state was home to the Eastern ___E:Algonquian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algonquian_peoples)___ tribes known as the Unami ___E:Lenape U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape)___ , or Delaware, who lived mostly along the coast, and the ___E:Nanticoke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanticoke_people)___ who occupied much of the southern ___E:Delmarva Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmarva_Peninsula)___ .

John Smith also shows two Iroquoian tribes, the Kuskarawock and ___E:Tockwogh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tockwogh)___ , living north of the Nanticoke—they may have held small portions of land in the western part of the state before migrating across the Chesapeake Bay.  The Kuskarawocks were most likely the ___E:Tuscarora U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuscarora_people)___ .

The Unami Lenape in the ___E:Delaware Valley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_Valley)___ were closely related to ___E:Munsee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munsee)___ Lenape tribes along the ___E:Hudson River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River)___ .

They had a settled hunting and agricultural society, and they rapidly became middlemen in an increasingly frantic fur trade with their ancient enemy, the Minqua or ___E:Susquehannock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susquehannock)___ .

With the loss of their lands on the ___E:Delaware River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River)___ and the destruction of the Minqua by the ___E:Iroquois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iroquois)___ of the Five Nations in the 1670s, the remnants of the Lenape who wished to remain identified as such left the region and moved over the ___E:Allegheny Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_Mountains)___ by the mid-18th century.

Generally, those who did not relocate out of the state of Delaware were baptized, became Christian and were grouped together with other persons of color in official records and in the minds of their non-Native American neighbors. [citation needed]

The ___E:Dutch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people)___ were the first Europeans to settle in present-day Delaware in the middle region by establishing a trading post at ___E:Zwaanendael U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zwaanendael,_Delaware)___ , near the site of ___E:Lewes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewes,_Delaware)___ in 1631.  Within a year, all the settlers were killed in a dispute with ___E:Native American tribes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States)___ living in the area. In 1638, ___E:New Sweden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Sweden)___ , a ___E:Swedish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_people)___ trading post and colony, was established at ___E:Fort Christina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Christina)___ (now in ___E:Wilmington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington,_Delaware)___ ) by ___E:Peter Minuit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Minuit)___ at the head of a group of Swedes, ___E:Finns U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_people)___ and Dutch.
The colony of New Sweden lasted 17 years.

In 1651, the Dutch, reinvigorated by the leadership of ___E:Peter Stuyvesant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Stuyvesant)___ , established a fort at present-day ___E:New Castle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Castle,_Delaware)___ and, in 1655, they conquered the New Sweden colony, annexing it into the Dutch ___E:New Netherland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Netherland)___ .

Only nine years later, in 1664, the Dutch were conquered by a fleet of English ships by Sir Robert Carr under the direction of ___E:James, the Duke of York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England)___ .

Fighting off a prior claim by ___E:Cecil Calvert, 2nd Baron Baltimore U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Calvert,_2nd_Baron_Baltimore)___ , ___E:Proprietor of Maryland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Maryland)___ , the Duke passed his somewhat dubious ownership on to ___E:William Penn U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Penn)___ in 1682. Penn strongly desired access to the sea for his ___E:Pennsylvania province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Pennsylvania)___ and leased what then came to be known as the "Lower Counties on the Delaware"  from the Duke.

Penn established representative government and briefly combined his two possessions under one General Assembly in 1682. However, by 1704 the province of Pennsylvania had grown so large their representatives wanted to make decisions without the assent of the Lower Counties, and the two groups of representatives began meeting on their own, one at ___E:Philadelphia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia)___ , and the other at New Castle.
Penn and his heirs remained proprietors of both and always appointed the same person Governor for their province of Pennsylvania and their territory of the Lower Counties.
The fact that Delaware and Pennsylvania shared the same governor was not unique; from 1703 to 1738, New York and New Jersey shared a governor.
Massachusetts and New Hampshire also shared a governor for some time.
Dependent in early years on indentured labor, Delaware imported more slaves as the number of English immigrants decreased with better economic conditions in England.
The colony became a slave society and cultivated tobacco as a cash crop, although English immigrants continued to arrive.
Like the other middle colonies, the Lower Counties on the Delaware initially showed little enthusiasm for a break with ___E:Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain)___ .
The citizenry had a good relationship with the Proprietary government, and generally were allowed more independence of action in their Colonial Assembly than in other colonies.
Merchants at the port of Wilmington had trading ties with the British.

New Castle lawyer ___E:Thomas McKean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_McKean)___ denounced the ___E:Stamp Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamp_Act_1765)___ in the strongest terms, and Kent County native ___E:John Dickinson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dickinson_(delegate))___ became the "Penman of the Revolution".

Anticipating the Declaration of Independence, ___E:Patriot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot_(American_Revolution))___ leaders Thomas McKean and ___E:Caesar Rodney U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar_Rodney)___ convinced the Colonial Assembly to declare itself separated from British and Pennsylvania rule on June 15, 1776. The person best representing Delaware's majority, ___E:George Read U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Read_(signer))___ , could not bring himself to vote for a Declaration of Independence.
Only the dramatic overnight ride of Caesar Rodney gave the delegation the votes needed to cast Delaware's vote for independence.

Initially led by ___E:John Haslet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Haslet)___ , Delaware provided one of the premier regiments in the ___E:Continental Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Army)___ , known as the "Delaware Blues" and nicknamed the " ___E:Blue Hen's Chicks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_Blue_Hen)___ ".

In August 1777 ___E:General Sir William Howe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Howe,_5th_Viscount_Howe)___ led a British army through Delaware on his way to a victory at the ___E:Battle of Brandywine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Brandywine)___ and capture of the city of Philadelphia.

The only real engagement on Delaware soil was the ___E:Battle of Cooch's Bridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cooch%27s_Bridge)___ , fought on September 3, 1777, at ___E:Cooch's Bridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooch%27s_Bridge)___ in New Castle County, although there was a ___E:minor Loyalist rebellion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clow_Rebellion)___ in 1778.

Following the Battle of Brandywine, Wilmington was occupied by the British, and ___E:State President U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Delaware)___ ___E:John McKinly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McKinly)___ was taken prisoner.

The British remained in control of the Delaware River for much of the rest of the war, disrupting commerce and providing encouragement to an active ___E:Loyalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyalist_(American_Revolution))___ portion of the population, particularly in Sussex County.
Because the British promised slaves of rebels freedom for fighting with them, escaped slaves flocked north to join their lines.

Following the ___E:American Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution)___ , statesmen from Delaware were among the leading proponents of a strong central United States with equal representation for each state.

Many colonial settlers came to Delaware from ___E:Maryland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland)___ and ___E:Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)___ , where the population had been increasing rapidly.

The economies of these colonies were chiefly based on labor-intensive tobacco and increasingly dependent on African ___E:slaves U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States)___ because of a decline in working class immigrants from England.

Most of the English colonists had arrived as ___E:indentured servants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indentured_servitude)___ (contracted for a fixed period to pay for their passage), and in the early years the line between servant and slave was fluid. [citation needed]

Most of the free African-American families in Delaware before the Revolution had migrated from Maryland to find more affordable land. They were descendants chiefly of relationships or marriages between white servant women and enslaved, servant or free African or African-American men.  Under slavery law, children took the social status of their mothers, so children born to white women were free, regardless of their paternity, just as children born to enslaved women were born into slavery.
As the flow of indentured laborers to the colony decreased with improving economic conditions in England, more slaves were imported for labor and the caste lines hardened.
By the end of the colonial period, the number of enslaved people in Delaware began to decline.
Shifts in the agriculture economy from tobacco to mixed farming resulted in less need for slaves' labor.

In addition local ___E:Methodists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist)___ and ___E:Quakers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaker)___ encouraged slaveholders to free their slaves following the American Revolution, and many did so in a surge of individual manumissions for idealistic reasons.
By 1810, three-quarters of all blacks in Delaware were free. When John Dickinson freed his slaves in 1777, he was Delaware's largest slave owner with 37 slaves.
In 1840, Delaware's population was 78,085 of whom 2,605 were slaves.
By 1860, the largest slaveholder owned 16 slaves.
Although attempts to abolish slavery failed by narrow margins in the legislature, in practical terms the state had mostly ended the practice.

By the ___E:1860 census U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census,_1860)___ on the verge of the ___E:Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War)___ , 91.7% of the black population were free;  1,798 were slaves, as compared to 19,829 "free colored persons".

An independent black denomination was chartered in 1813 by freed slave ___E:Peter Spencer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Spencer_(religious_leader))___ as the " ___E:Union Church of Africans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Churches)___ ".

This followed the 1793 establishment in Philadelphia of the ___E:African Methodist Episcopal Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Methodist_Episcopal_Church)___ by ___E:Richard Allen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Allen_(bishop))___ , which had ties to the Methodist Episcopal Church until 1816. Spencer built a church in Wilmington for the new denomination.

This was renamed as the ___E:African Union First Colored Methodist Protestant Church and Connection U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union_First_Colored_Methodist_Protestant_Church_and_Connection)___ , more commonly known as the ___E:A.U.M.P. Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A.U.M.P._Church)___ .

In 1814, Spencer called for the first annual gathering, known as the ___E:Big August Quarterly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_August_Quarterly)___ , which continues to draw members of this denomination and their descendants together in a religious and cultural festival.
Delaware voted against ___E:secession U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession)___ on January 3, 1861, and so remained in the Union.

While most Delaware citizens who fought in the war served in the regiments of the state, some served in companies on the Confederate side in ___E:Maryland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maryland_Confederate_Civil_War_units)___ and ___E:Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Virginia_Civil_War_units)___ Regiments.

Delaware is notable for being the only slave state from which no Confederate regiments or militia groups were assembled. [citation needed] Delaware essentially freed the few slaves who were still in bondage shortly after the Civil War [further explanation needed] but rejected the ___E:13th U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ , ___E:14th U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ , and ___E:15th U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ Amendments to the Constitution; the 13th Amendment was rejected on February 8, 1865, the 14th Amendment was rejected on February 8, 1867, and the 15th Amendment was rejected on March 18, 1869. Delaware officially ratified the 13th, 14th, and 15th amendments on February 12, 1901, decades after they had already come into force.

During the ___E:Reconstruction Era U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era_of_the_United_States)___ that followed the ___E:Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War)___ , Democratic ___E:Redeemer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redeemers)___ governments led by the South's ___E:Bourbon aristocracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourbon_Democrats)___ continued to dominate the region and imposed explicitly ___E:white supremacist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacist)___ regimes in the former slave states.

The Delaware legislature declared Black people to be second-class citizens in 1866, and restricted their voting rights despite the 15th Amendment, ensuring continued Democratic success in the state throughout most of the 19th century.

Fearful that the ___E:1875 Civil Rights Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1875_Civil_Rights_Act)___ passed by Congress might establish racial equality, Delaware legislators passed ___E:Jim Crow laws U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow_laws)___ that mandated ___E:segregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation)___ in public facilities.

The state's educational system was segregated by operation of law.  Delaware's segregation was written into the state constitution, which, while providing at Article X, Section 2, that "no distinction shall be made on account of race or color", nonetheless required that "separate schools for white and colored children shall be maintained."
Beginning in the late 19th century, the Wilmington area grew into a manufacturing center.

Investment in manufacturing in the city grew from $5.5 million in 1860 to $44 million in 1900.  The most notable manufacturer in the state was the chemical company ___E:DuPont U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuPont)___ , which to this day is heavily credited with making the state what it is today in many ways.  Because of Wilmington's growth, local politicians from the city and New Castle County pressured the state government to adopt a new constitution providing the north with more representation.
However, the subsequent 1897 constitution did not proportionally represent the north and continued to give the southern counties disproportionate influence.
As manufacturing expanded, businesses became major players in state affairs and funders of politicians through families such as the Du Ponts.

Republican ___E:John Addicks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Edward_Addicks)___ attempted to buy a US Senate seat multiple times in a rivalry with the Du Ponts until the passage of the ___E:17th Amendment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventeenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution)___ .
The allegiance of industries with the Republican party allowed them to gain control of the state's governorship throughout most of the 20th century.
The GOP ensured black people could vote because of their general support for Republicans and thus undid restrictions on Black suffrage.
Delaware benefited greatly from World War I because of the state's large gunpowder industry.

DuPont, the most dominant business in the state by WWI, produced an estimated 40% of all gunpowder used by the Allies during the war. It produced nylon in the state after the war and began investments into ___E:General Motors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors)___ .

Additionally, the company invested heavily in the expansion of public schools in the state and colleges such as the ___E:University of Delaware U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Delaware)___ in the 1910s and 1920s.
This included primary and secondary schools for Black people and women.

Delaware suffered less during the ___E:Great Depression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression)___ than other states, but the depression spurred further migration from the rural south to urban areas.

Like in World War I, the state enjoyed a big stimulus to its gunpowder and shipyard industries in World War II. New job opportunities during and after the war in the Wilmington area coaxed Black people from the southern counties to move to the city. The proportion of blacks constituting the city's population rose from 15% in 1950 to over 50% by 1980.  The surge of Black migrants to the north sparked ___E:white flight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight)___ , in which middle class whites moved from the city to suburban areas, leading to de facto segregation of Northern Delaware's society.

In the 1940s and 1950s, Delaware attempted to integrate its schools, although the last segregated school in the state did not close until 1970.  The ___E:University of Delaware U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Delaware)___ admitted its first black student in 1948, and local courts ruled that primary schools had to be integrated.

Delaware's integration efforts partially inspired the US Supreme Court's decision in Brown v. Board of Education , which found racial segregation in United States ___E:public schools U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_school)___ to be unconstitutional.
The result of the Brown ruling was that Delaware became fully integrated, albeit with time and much effort.

In October 1954, the city of ___E:Milford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford,_Delaware)___ became the scene of one of the country's first pro-segregation ___E:boycotts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boycotts)___ after eleven Black students were enrolled in the previously all-white ___E:Milford High School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_High_School_(Delaware))___ .
Mass protests continued in Milford; the school board eventually ceded to the protestors, expelling the Black students.

The ensuing unrest, which included ___E:cross burnings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_burning)___ , rallies, and pro-segregation demonstrations, contributed to ___E:desegregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desegregation_in_the_United_States)___ in most of Southern Delaware being delayed for another ten years. ___E:Sussex County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex_County,_Delaware)___ did not start closing or integrating its segregated schools until 1965, 11 years after the Brown ruling.
Throughout the state, integration only encouraged more white flight, and poor economic conditions for the black population led to some violence during the 1960s.

Riots broke out in Wilmington in 1967 and again in ___E:1968 in response to the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington_riot_of_1968)___ , after which the National Guard occupied the city for nine months to prevent further violence.

Since WWII, the state has been generally economically prosperous and enjoyed relatively high per capita income because of its location between major cities like Philadelphia, New York, and Washington, DC.  Its population grew rapidly, particularly in the suburbs in the north where New Castle county became an extension of the ___E:Philadelphia metropolitan area U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_metropolitan_area)___ .
Americans, including migrants from Puerto Rico, and immigrants from Latin America flocked to the state.
By 1990, only 50% of Delaware's population consisted of natives to the state.

Delaware is 96 miles (154 km) long and ranges from 9 to 35 miles (14 to 56 km) across, with a land area of 1,982 square miles (5,130 km 2 )  and a total area of 2,489 square miles (6,450 km 2 ),  making it the second-smallest state by either metric in the United States after ___E:Rhode Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island)___ .

Delaware is bounded to the north by ___E:Pennsylvania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania)___ ; to the east by the ___E:Delaware River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River)___ , ___E:Delaware Bay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_Bay)___ , ___E:New Jersey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey)___ , and the Atlantic Ocean; and to the west and south by ___E:Maryland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland)___ .
Small portions of Delaware are also situated on the eastern side of the Delaware River sharing land boundaries with New Jersey.

[b] Although the Twelve-Mile Circle is often claimed to be the only territorial boundary in the U.S. that is a true ___E:arc U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_(geometry))___ , the Mexican boundary with Texas includes several arcs,  and many cities in the South (such as ___E:Plains, Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plains,_Georgia)___ )  also have circular boundaries.

This border extends all the way east to the low-tide mark on the New Jersey shore, then continues south along the shoreline until it again reaches the 12-mile (19 km) arc in the south; then the boundary continues in a more conventional way in the middle of the main channel ( ___E:thalweg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalweg)___ ) of the Delaware River.

The border follows the Circle for a short distance and then continues in a straight line due north until reaching the southern border of Pennsylvania.  ___E:The Wedge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wedge_(border))___ of land between the northwest part of the arc and the Maryland border was claimed by both Delaware and Pennsylvania until 1921, when Delaware's claim was confirmed.
